The anti-immigrant AfD party has been making significant gains Image: Sonam Mishra/DW Advertisement Abdu Taviq, an Egyptian software developer, ended up in Germany's capital more or less by chance seven years ago. "I wouldn't say I chose Berlin," he told DW. "It was just that the company that offered me a job was here." But now he loves it. The culture is "better than any other city I have experienced," he said. That's partly because of its diversity, but he also likes the way Berliners approach life. "They're more interested in living than just working," he said. "Here I feel life is more relaxed, and this also offers the opportunity for people to get more creative." But there's plenty about the city that he's not particularly happy with, including Berlin 's rapidly rising rental prices, and the notoriously opaque bureaucracy is a constant source of annoyance. "I myself would like to start my own business, but it is difficult because of all the bureaucracy," he said. In general, Taviq is dissatisfied with Berlin's current government, a conservative-led coalition of the Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) — but the trouble is, as a non-German national, he has no say in deciding whether it should stay in office or not. That is particularly frustrating at the moment, when the streets are bristling with campaign posters ahead of the election on September 20. "We are people who pay taxes, but we don't have any representation at all, even on local level," he said. "The cuts to kindergartens and German courses, for example, affect me directly." Berlin initiative helps immigrant moms find their feet To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Berlin: Bigger and more international The German capital is growing and becoming more international. While the voting population in the upcoming election will be bigger than ever — mainly because the voting age has been lowered to 16 — so is the number of the disenfranchised. Of Berlin's population of 3.9 million, a full quarter — around 976,000 adults — cannot vote because they don't have German citizenship . That number has doubled since 2011. This is partly because of Germany's political structure. In Germany and across Europe, citizens of other EU countries can vote in municipal elections. In London, people from Commonwealth countries can do the same as long as they have UK residency. Spain, meanwhile, also has reciprocal voting agreements with several non-EU countries — in South America and elsewhere — that allow their citizens to vote in municipal elections, including for the mayors of Madrid and Barcelona. Berlin's upcoming election is not a municipal one. Since Berlin is one of Germany's 16 federal states, this will be a state election, which means that voting rights are more restricted. Berlin's municipal elections, where EU citizens are allowed to vote, only decide who governs the city's individual districts, and their political influence is limited. The disenfranchisement is particularly acute in central Berlin. For that reason, Stefanie Remlinger, Green Party mayor in the district of Mitte, has organized a "symbolic election" for the non-Germans in her area — some 135,000 adults out of a population of 365,000. The initiative invites foreigners to vote at 15 ballot stations over a two-week period in early September to "raise awareness for the issue of voting rights for all." "Mitte is an extremely heterogeneous district with a very international population," Remlinger told DW via video call from her office. "We have people from 170 different countries living here, and a lot of them don't have the right to vote. It's important to us to signal to those people that we value their opinions, that we see them." Around a third of adults in Stefanie Remlinger's district don't have German nationality Image: Annette Hauschild Germany's 'rightward shift' Getting people to vote in a meaningless election is a tough sell. Remlinger said she expected only a few hundred people to take part, and, anyway, she thinks the political climate in Germany is not exactly immigrant-friendly at the moment. Even in cosmopolitan Berlin, the anti-immigrant Alternative for Germany (AfD) is currently polling in second place, with nearly 20%. "We as the Greens would liberalize voting rights even more, but I don't see the general debate in Germany going that way," she said. "We're fighting a rightward shift and a lot of hostility to immigration, and I think the chances of changing something on that issue right now are very bad." To illustrate the state of the current debate, Remlinger mentioned a recent panel discussion she was part of, where a politician from the neoliberal Free Democratic Party (FDP) — a party that calls itself socially liberal — said voting rights shouldn't be opened to foreigners because they might start their own parties and take over the government. "And that from someone from the FDP!" said Remlinger, exasperated. Taviq is also aware of this anti-immigrant shift in German politics. In fact, he said, that was one of the reasons he was considering leaving Germany altogether. "All the parties are trending right-wing, so it's getting more hostile," he said. How Berliners are reshaping their city for the future To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Is expanding voting good for the economy? From an economic perspective, it might be considered a shame if qualified people like Taviq decided to leave Germany. The country lacks workers. The government estimates that the country will be short of about 440,000 workers by 2029, and even the AfD leadership claims it has nothing against immigrants who contribute to the economy. Though some German cities and local authorities do have an elected advisory board for non-German residents, offering immigrants a real vote is frequently seen as a step too far. Remlinger herself thinks that the best path to enfranchisement is not to offer foreign nationals voting rights, but to make it easier for immigrants to become German citizens. That happens to be another one of Taviq's complaints about Berlin: "I applied for citizenship two years ago, and I didn't get any response," he said. Germany has recently tightened citizenship rules again. Last year, Chancellor Friedrich Merz 's government reversed the three-year "fast-track" citizenship option introduced under his predecessor, Olaf Scholz. Still, the government did keep another of Scholz's reforms, which allows people to apply for citizenship after only five years of residency. More and more Berliners are in fact becoming German: 2025 saw about 39,000 people naturalized in the capital, 17,000 more than in 2024. That avenue is still closed for Taviq, but in the meantime, a little more political participation would go a long way. "If I could vote, I would reconsider leaving, to be honest, because then I could affect things, but now I'm just like a bank machine — they come to me and take half of my salary." https://www.dw.com/en/us-imposes-sanctio.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5O4Qb The US has had the ICC on its radar more or less throughout the second Trump term Image: John Thys/AFP Advertisement US President Donald Trump 's administration imposed sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) on Friday, hours after one of its former judges won the Nobel Peace Prize. This comes as the US has in recent months made no bones about pursuing what Secretary of State Marco Rubio has called a "sweeping campaign to dismantle the threat posed by the International Criminal Court." The United States and Israel had both strongly opposed the court's arrest warrants for top Israeli officials, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu . Since 2020 and the back end of Trump's first term, the US had also opposed investigations into military actions in Afghanistan that "deprioritize" alleged US wrongdoings, focusing on the Taliban, but can nevertheless include them. ICC judges living under US sanctions To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video What did the State Department say about the ICC sanctions? "President Trump will never allow the International Court to prosecute Americans," Rubio said in a statement . "That is why, today, the United States is sanctioning the International Criminal Court. We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate," he said. Rubio said that both US political parties had long agreed that the ICC should not have jurisdiction over US citizens, but said "only President Trump" resolved to take action. "Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC. We expect our allies, many of whom are part of the ICC and that rely on American servicemembers for their defense, to rein in the court," Rubio said. "If they do not, the United States will continue its campaign to dismantle the ICC, brick by brick, until Americans are threatened no longer." ICC President Tomoko Akane was sanctioned by the US in August Image: Eva Plevier/ANP/AFP How did the ICC respond? The ICC said the US sanctions aimed to obstruct an independent international court supported by more than half of the UN's members. "The court will continue to fully discharge its mandate, with independence and impartiality, acting only on the basis of the law and the evidence, for the sake of the countless victims of grave crimes," said ICC President Tomoko Akane, who already faces US sanctions . The ICC called the Rome Statute, which underpins membership of the court, a "collective promise" that the most serious international crimes must not go unpunished. "That promise is only as strong as the resolve of those who made it," the court said. It appealed to members to take "concrete actions" to ensure the court would still have the necessary means to continue its work. "No one should be punished for serving the cause of justice," it said. "History will judge this moment. Future generations, and above all the victims of mass atrocities, will ask how we responded when an insitution created to protect them came under attack." The US announcement came just hours after Navi Pillay, a former ICC judge, was given this year's Nobel Peace Prize Image: Daniel Karmann/dpa/picture alliance What did other countries say about the US sanctions? A collection of US allies that are full members of the ICC including Germany issued a joint statement reaffirming their "continued and unwavering support for the independence, impartiality, and integrity of the ICC." "As committed supporters of the ICC we regret and strongly disagree with the announcement of sanctions to be imposed upon the Court by the United States," the governments of Canada, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands and the UK said . They said that, despite the ICC's best efforts to prepare and mitigate their effect, the sanctions "will have a significant impact on the Court's work, its dedicated staff and their families." Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu thanked the US government for its "leadership" in issuing the sanctions. "The ICC is not a court. It is a political body that poses a mortal threat to law abiding democracies worldwide and to the very idea of national sovereignty," he said. Sanctions announced shortly after former ICC judge's Nobel Peace Prize The State Department released the announcement a few hours after the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize was awarded to Navi Pillay, who was an ICC judge from 2003 to 2012. Last year Trump repeatedly complained that he should have won the accolade for promoting world peace, prompting Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado to present him with her trophy as a gift . Without naming names, the Nobel Committee clearly referenced US sanctions against the ICC when announcing Pillay as this year's laureate. "The Norwegian Nobel Committee wants to remind the world that the rule of law national and international — underpins the system we have set up to ensure peace and resolve conflicts non-violently," the Committee wrote. It said judges like Pillay "guard the thin red line between order and chaos," but lamented that "today ... these same judges are sanctioned, and their institutions are attacked." What is the ICC? The International Criminal Court is an intergovernmental organization and international tribunal based in the Dutch city of The Hague. It's the only permanent international court with the theoretical jurisdiction to prosecute individuals for international crimes like genocide , crimes against humanity, war crimes and illegal aggression. The ICC was established in 2002 and is governed by the Rome Statute. More than half the countries in the world, 125 in total, are full parties to the Rome Statute, having signed and ratified it. Several of the world's most significant powers, including China, India, Israel, Russia and the United States, do not recognize the court's jurisdiction and are not parties to the statute. A grey area, however, remains since the court accepts challenges from ratified members against individuals from countries that do not recognize it. That is why high-profile arrest warrants against Russian officials, including President Vladimir Putin, and Israeli officials, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, have been issued in recent years — following respective complaints from Ukrainians and Palestinians. What were the prior signs of Trump administration pressure on the ICC? The US has been increasingly critical of the ICC during Trump's second term. Rubio has often led the charge. In July, he wrote an op-ed for the Wall Street Journal saying, "America never agreed to a world tribunal that can override our own courts and the Constitution." He argued it was possible for US "soldiers, police officers, Border Patrol agents and elected leaders" to be "dragged before an international court" and tried by judges "from random countries across the globe." Just over a week later, on July 25, Venezuela's new administration — transformed after the US abduction of Nicolas Maduro in January — announced that it planned to withdraw from the Rome Statute and the ICC. A few days later, the military junta in Chad announced that it was withdrawing from the ICC following a US request. The recent sexual misconduct scandal surrounding the ICC's chief prosecutor Karim Khan , who was dismissed in July, provided more ammunition the US could aim at the court. In August, the US imposed sanctions on the ICC's president, Japanese judge Tomoko Akane, and Abdoulaye Seye, a Senegalese trial lawyer at the court. Speaking at the UN General Assembly last month, Donald Trump branded the ICC 'evil,' but stopped short of announcing sanctions even as reports of the plan circulated Image: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Photo/picture alliance If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google , so you'll always see our verified news first. Photograph: Ryan Murphy/AP View image in fullscreen Selma Blair leaves court on 12 October 2026 in New York after her arraignment on charges of injuring two flight attendants during a cross-country flight. Photograph: Ryan Murphy/AP Selma Blair Selma Blair ‘did not intend to harm anyone’ during airplane incident, representatives say Actor experienced a ‘medical emergency’ on flight during which she allegedly injured crew members, statement says Ramon Antonio Vargas and agencies Sat 17 Oct 2026 09.52 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Actor Selma Blair did not mean to hurt anyone during the recent flight which led to her arrest on allegations that she assaulted a pair of cabin crew members, a police officer and a nurse, her representatives said on Friday in a statement that characterized the episode as a medical emergency. The lengthy statement also dismissed prior media coverage of Blair’s arrest after a Delta Air Lines flight from Los Angeles to New York as unsympathetic and inaccurate, singling out reporting from several outlets alleging that she tried to open the door of the airplane that she and her fellow passengers were on. “Selma Blair experienced a medical emergency on the flight,” her representatives’ statement contended. “There was no attempt to open the door of the aircraft. Selma did not intend to harm anyone.” Selma Blair charged with assault of police officer and nurse after allegedly attacking flight attendants Read more Friday’s statement from Blair’s camp added some contours to brief remarks made in the days since her arrest by her publicist and lawyer which maintained that there had been a medical emergency but did not elaborate much. Without specifying who may have done so, the statement on Friday called it “outrageous” for anyone to suggest Blair does not have multiple sclerosis (MS), a chronic neurological disorder which she went public about being diagnosed with in 2018. “What Selma has been able to do physically in the years since is nothing short of a miracle,” said the statement, which was reported by the Associated Press and People . “She still has bad days, and she lives with pain daily.” The statement said Blair has a condition secondary to her MS known as pseudobulbar affect, “which bears directly on how a medical episode presents to people who do not know her”. Blair therefore “travels with a service dog who doesn’t leave her side”. “And the authorities took her dog from her,” said the statement, which described Blair as a disability rights and MS community advocate. Blair’s statement faulted media outlets which – in covering her arrest on Sunday – referred to a 2016 incident in which she reportedly began screaming uncontrollably while on a Los Angeles-bound flight from Cancún, Mexico, before being removed on a stretcher. The actor apologized after that earlier incident, saying that she “mixed alcohol with medication”, blacking out as a result while saying and doing things that “I deeply regret”. Blair’s representatives expressed gratitude to the “handful of journalists [who] have taken the time to report on Selma as a human being rather than a headline”. “Fair reporting has been the exception,” said their statement on Friday, which accused the media of building a narrative around Blair almost solely on police allegations “and a decade-old headline”. “There is much more to this than has been reported,” the statement continued, without offering specifics. “And we ask to consider the entirety of the facts before rushing to judgment, whether in the courtroom or in the court of public opinion.” Authorities accused Blair of injuring two flight attendants while traveling from LA to the John F Kennedy airport (JFK) in New York on Sunday night. She also was alleged to have kicked a police officer taking her to the hospital and kicking a nurse once she arrived at the facility, said a statement from the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey, which operates JFK. She pleaded not guilty on Monday to state assault charges involving the officer and the nurse, with a judge ordering Blair to stay away from them. Blair was freed on bail and tentatively scheduled to return to court in January. Meanwhile, the AP reported that Blair had gotten a notice from the FBI charging her with assault for alleged actions on Delta flight 938. The outlet cited a federal law enforcement official who spoke on the condition of anonymity for not being authorized to speak publicly about the case. Details of exactly what happened in the moments leading up to Blair’s arrest haven’t been disclosed by Delta, state authorities or the FBI. An air traffic control audio recording from the flight Blair was on captured the pilot saying: “One flight attendant and one passenger … sustained some minor injuries – a bloody nose as well as some bite marks.” “I don’t think we need an ambulance or anything like that – but we just want to get some medical personnel at the gate to look at their injuries,” the pilot said, according to the recording, a copy of which was published by NBC Los Angeles. Beside that case and the incident in 2016, Blair grappled with controversy when she apologized in February 2024 for an Islamophobic comment on social media. Blair’s major film credits include Cruel Intentions in 1999, Legally Blonde in 2001 and Hellboy in 2004. She earned a 2011 Grammy award nomination for best spoken word album for children for her work on Anne Frank: The Diary of a Young Girl – The Definitive Edition. And she also starred in the acclaimed 2021 documentary Introducing, Selma Blair, which explores her life after her MS diagnosis. Photograph: Chris J Ratcliffe/Reuters Metropolitan police Detective raped by fellow officer David Carrick calls on Met chief to resign Linda Williams, who was attacked in 2004, says force’s handling of her case was ‘like being raped all over again’ Jamie Grierson Fri 23 Oct 2026 05.42 EDT Last modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 06.06 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A detective who was raped by the former Scotland Yard officer David Carrick has called for the head of the Metropolitan police to resign, saying the handling of her case was “like being raped all over again”. Linda Williams, 60, who has waived her right to anonymity, was attacked by Carrick in 2004. She launched a legal case against the Met for failing to protect her against the serial rapist, and has now settled for an undisclosed six-figure sum without the force admitting liability. Carrick, 51, who previously served as an armed officer in the Met, is one of the country’s worst sex offenders and is serving 37 life sentences after attacking more than a dozen women. View image in fullscreen David Carrick. Photograph: Hertfordshire police/PA Williams, from Hertfordshire, has said the way she was treated by the force throughout her legal claim was “devastating” and that it drove her to contemplate suicide. “The whole process has taken me right back to how I felt when I was raped by Carrick: controlled, abused and powerless,” she said. “If I was raped tomorrow, I wouldn’t report it. Both the criminal justice process and the civil process have been so traumatic. “I say that as someone who was once a sexual offences officer, supporting victims myself. Despite that experience and my understanding of the system, I still wouldn’t report it, because of the complete lack of empathy and support I have experienced from the police. “At no point did I feel they sincerely acknowledged that I had been through a horrific sexual attack and that the trauma of that had deeply scarred me, or their role in it all.” Williams brought a civil case against the Met seeking damages on the basis that the force failed to protect her from Carrick and that she felt she had been unable to report the rape. She said the Met’s legal team in the case questioned the severity of her post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) diagnosis. “They used the fact that I just got on with my life as best I could after the rape against me,” she said. “I was an exemplary officer and continued to perform well at work, and they relied on that to suggest I had shown no signs of psychological trauma. “As far as I am concerned, it is Mark Rowley , the [Met] commissioner, saying these terrible things, as he was the defendant in the case.” She said the Met needed to set up a unit overseen by victims like herself who understood what it was like to be raped. “For this to happen Rowley needs to go and we need a new commissioner,” she said. Williams alleged it was the “Met’s fault” that she could not report the rape in 2004, and that “little had changed” in the culture since then. She added that the force was “like an episode of Life On Mars”, the 2000s TV drama set in a fictional 1970s police station. She said: “I wouldn’t have had the backup of my colleagues in dangerous situations and ultimately, I doubt anything would have been done about Carrick.” Williams reported the rape in 2021, and said she had had no relationships since the attack, 22 years ago. “After the attack, I couldn’t face the thought of being with a man or even having somebody in my home. That makes for a lonely Christmas and no holidays. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion “It’s my choice, but the reason behind it wasn’t my choice. That’s down to the attack. Carrick stole the future that I wanted.” Williams told the BBC the PTSD she had experienced after the attack was “90% down to the Met police, 10% to Carrick”. In 2022 and 2023, Carrick pleaded guilty to 71 sexual offences , including 48 rapes against 12 other women over 17 years. In November last year, he was convicted of molesting a 12-year-old child in the late 1980s and repeatedly raping and abusing a female ex-partner. A Met spokesperson said: “Serious flaws in the way we approached such investigations at the time meant we did not spot his pattern of abusive behaviour. “As a result, we missed opportunities to pursue him through the misconduct process. We deeply regret this. We recognise the unique and additional impact on DC Linda Williams, whose exposure to Carrick came as a result of her being a Met officer. “Her continued commitment to public service, in spite of the trauma she experienced, is commendable. Throughout subsequent legal proceedings, the Met has tried to reduce further distress and re-traumatisation to DC Williams’ welfare and has aimed to deal with her claims as quickly and compassionately as possible. “The commissioner has previously met with DC Williams in person as well as spoken to her via email on multiple occasions. He has repeatedly acknowledged that she has shown courage in speaking out about her experience in an effort to drive forward necessary change and in now waiving her anonymity to continue to do so. “He has contacted DC Williams to ask whether she would be willing to meet again and further discuss these issues in person.” Explore more on these topics Metropolitan police Rape and sexual assault Violence against women and girls Police Mark Rowley England London news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed UK UK politics Education Media Society Law Scotland Wales Northern Ireland

Photograph: Ukrainian Emergency Service/AP View image in fullscreen Rescuers evacuate a wounded commuter after a Russian drone attack killed at least 14 people and injured others on a railway platform in Dnipro, Ukraine. Photograph: Ukrainian Emergency Service/AP Russia-Ukraine war at a glance Russia Explainer Ukraine war briefing: Outrage in Europe after Russian drone kills 14 on rail platform in Dnipro EU council president calls deadly strike ‘cruel and devastating’; fragile ceasefire holds in Oleshky. What we know on day 1,710 Guardian staff and agencies Thu 29 Oct 2026 22.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google European leaders have reacted with outrage to a deadly attack by a Russian drone that slammed into a busy railway platform in the Ukrainian city of Dnipro on Thursday, as Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned Ukraine had intelligence about more ballistic missile strikes to come. French President Emmanuel Macron stressed the need for “far more than a localised ceasefire”, referencing the current truce in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky. The EU council president, António Costa, who described the Dnipro attacks as “cruel and devastating”, called for greater pressure on Russia after the latest strikes against civilians. “The EU will continue to increase the pressure on Russia and to support Ukraine until a just and lasting peace is achieved,” he added. “We call on all our international partners to do the same.” Later on Thursday, Russian forces ⁠launched ⁠an attack ​on the ⁠Ukrainian capital ⁠Kyiv ​with ‌ballistic ‌missiles , Mayor Vitali Klitschko ‌said on Telegram, hitting warehouses and ‌triggering a fire. Emergency services were headed to ​the scene on the east side ⁠of the Dnipro ​River, he said. Describing the Dnipro train station attack – which killed at least 14 people and injured another 14 – as “horrific”, the president of Ukraine insisted “sanctions against Moscow and its war machine must not be eased for as long as this Russian war continues”. Zelenskyy warned also that Ukraine had intelligence about preparations by the Russians of new ballistic missile strikes. “We need the means to take out all this Russian ‌evil. We are expecting relevant decisions,” he said. Another attack on Dnipro hit a student dormitory, setting it ablaze, regional governor Oleksandr Hanzha said, adding the assaults had cut power to 350,000 households. The strikes came as Ukraine and Russia kept to a fragile local ceasefire in the ravaged city of Oleshky – under Russian occupation since 2022 and where residents have faced months of food, water and medicine shortages. While the truce held into a third day, strikes elsewhere in Ukraine killed at least 20 people and injured more than 70 people, according to local officials. Russia and Ukraine said on Thursday an operation to bring aid into the town and allow ⁠residents to leave was ready to begin. Meanwhile, Ukraine’s military ⁠has paused its strikes on Russian oil refineries after pressure from US President Donald Trump , ⁠according to a report in the Wall Street ⁠Journal ​on Thursday, citing people with knowledge of the operations. Ukrainian units carrying out ⁠long-range strikes were told in mid-October that the campaign against refineries was effectively on hold once ⁠missions already in motion were completed, the Journal reported. The ​unofficial pause is expected ‌to last until ‌after the US midterm elections and potentially deeper into ‌November, the newspaper said. After the Dnipro attack, Zelenskyy renewed his criticism of a deal struck between Trump and Russia’s President Vladimir Putin to ease some US sanctions on Russia allowing Moscow to release diesel on to global markets. “How many such terrorist strikes has Russia carried out against our people since sanctions were lifted on some Russian oligarchs and the energy sector, instead of de-escalating?” he asked. Late on Thursday, Putin said he supported any steps aimed at restoring relations with ⁠European countries, saying the outbreak of any conflict would leave ⁠a situation with ⁠no ​winners . Commenting on his phone call this week with the leaders of Norway and Finland , Putin told reporters after ‌hosting a summit with African ‌leaders: “And if anyone wants it, let them prepare, but right now they have not achieved their goal – to inflict a strategic defeat on Russia. And if things go too far, there will be no winners at all. .” Explore more on these topics Russia Russia-Ukraine war at a glance Ukraine Europe Trump administration Emmanuel Macron Volodymyr Zelenskyy explainers Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development
